sections.html: Appleton is the seat of Outagamie County, on the Fox River about 30 miles southwest of Green Bay. The 2020 census counted 75,644 residents in 24.82 square miles. Most of the city lies in Outagamie County, with smaller pieces in Calumet and Winnebago counties, and the city sits in five school districts. That split affects you in two ways: the Assessor keeps more than one tax rate and assessment level, and delinquent tax goes to a different county treasurer depending on where your parcel falls.

sections.h2: Who assesses and who bills property tax in Appleton?
sections.html:
The city handles both jobs, split between two offices. The county steps in only when a bill goes delinquent.

  • Assessor's Office, (920) 832-5850. Values every parcel, keeps ownership and lot descriptions, and mails a notice when an assessment changes. All property is revalued at least once every five years, and the office tries to inspect each property at least once every ten.
  • Finance Department, (920) 832-6442. Bills and collects tax at City Hall, 100 N. Appleton St. On weekdays you can pay at the first-floor desk or the drive-up window, use the night deposit box, mail a check to P.O. Box 2519, Appleton, WI 54912-2519, or pay online through the Payment Center. The online processor adds a convenience fee that the city never receives.
  • City Clerk, (920) 832-6443. Takes notices of intent to object and objection forms for the Board of Review.

The Finance page on the city website carries a copy of your bill and a breakdown of where the money goes. Your tax is the net rate per $1,000 times your assessed value. The rate comes from the combined budgets of the school district, city, county, sewer district, technical college and state reforestation.

Owners can pay in four installments, due January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31, with the dates printed on the bill. State law has bills out by the third Monday in December. If any installment is late, the installment option is cancelled and monthly interest runs from February 1 on the unpaid balance. Wis. Stat. 74.47 sets that interest at one percent a month, and a county board may add a penalty of up to half a percent a month.

Once a balance is delinquent, the city stops collecting it. Unpaid balances from 2025 and earlier years go to the county treasurer for the county where the parcel sits.

Refunds work like this. If you pay in person with an escrow check and are owed $750 or less, you may get the refund in cash. Larger refunds, and any refund on a mailed or drop-box payment, are mailed within four to six weeks. Escrow checks made out to both the owner and the City of Appleton need both endorsements.

sections.h2: How the Appleton assessment and appeal process works
sections.html:
Each spring the city mails a Notice of Changed Assessment, then holds an informal Open Book review ahead of the formal Board of Review. Once the board meets, that year's assessments are final. Ask the Assessor for the calendar for the coming year. State law requires the notice at least 15 days before the board meets, or 30 days in a revaluation year.

To object, follow the steps the Clerk lists:

  • Talk to the Assessor first. The Clerk calls this step one.
  • Tell the City Clerk, in writing or by voice, that you intend to object, at least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting.
  • File Objection Form PA-115A within the first two hours of that first meeting.
  • Bring evidence. The Board starts from the view that the assessor is right, and the burden sits with the owner.

The board has seven members: the Mayor, the City Clerk, three alderpersons and three residents. A decision can go to circuit court by certiorari within 90 days of the notice of decision under Wis. Stat. 70.47.

By the time the December bill arrives, it is too late to object. Paying under protest is not an objection unless you first appealed to the Board of Review.

sections.h2: Which credits reduce an Appleton tax bill?
sections.html:
Two state credits show up on the bill. The lottery and gaming credit goes to an owner who used the home as a primary residence on January 1 of the year taxes are levied, and the amount changes each year. The first dollar credit is applied automatically to every taxable parcel with an improvement on it, whether or not the owner lives there. Ask the county treasurer for your county about the lottery credit.

What you do to the house can also move the assessment. Routine work such as a new furnace, roof repair, gutters or patched walls generally does not raise it, though several items together might. Additions, finished basements, new decks and extensive kitchen or bath remodels usually do. Assessors visit recently sold homes in the fall and winter, so expect a letter after a sale.

sections.h2: What fees apply when I sell an Appleton house?
sections.html:
Wisconsin charges the seller a real estate transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value, under Wis. Stat. 77.22. The Register of Deeds collects it when the deed is recorded, and buyer and seller must first sign an electronic transfer return. Whether Outagamie, Calumet or Winnebago County does the recording depends on where the parcel sits.

Some conveyances are exempt under Wis. Stat. 77.25, and the reason must be written on the face of the deed. Examples include transfers by will, descent or survivorship, foreclosure transfers and deeds in lieu to the mortgage holder, sales for delinquent taxes, and transfers between parent and child or grandparent and grandchild for little or no payment. An ordinary sale to a buyer is not on the list.

sections.h2: Clearing unpaid Appleton property tax before a sale
sections.html:
Have the title or escrow company order a payoff from the correct treasurer. For the current bill that is the Finance Department. For 2025 and earlier years it is the county treasurer, and the payoff includes interest from February 1. Under Wisconsin's delinquent tax statutes, delinquent real property tax can be discharged by paying the amount with interest and any penalty before a tax certificate is issued on the parcel.

Do not wait for the bill if a closing will fall near a deadline. Tell your closing agent which installments are paid. If the house has been in the family for years and the tax history is murky, call the Finance Department with the parcel number, which is the fastest way to learn what is open.

The tax side of an Appleton sale follows a short sequence.

  • Find your parcel number and note which county it sits in.
  • Ask Finance at (920) 832-6442 which installments are paid on the current bill.
  • If any earlier year is open, call the county treasurer from the table above for a payoff with interest.
  • Check whether an assessment notice arrived recently, and if you plan to object, remember the Board of Review calendar.
  • Give the closing agent the payoff letters so the balances can be paid from your proceeds.

A cash buyer can shorten the timeline because there is no lender underwriting, yet the transfer return, the recording and the tax payoff all remain.

faqs.q: When are Appleton property taxes due?
faqs.a: In four installments on January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. Missing one cancels the installment option and starts interest from February 1. Pay at City Hall, by mail, in a drop box or online.

faqs.q: Which county treasurer do I pay if my Appleton taxes are delinquent?
faqs.a: The treasurer for the county where the parcel sits: Outagamie at (920) 832-5065, Calumet at (920) 849-1457 or Winnebago at (920) 232-3420. The city sends unpaid balances for 2025 and earlier years there.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Appleton assessment?
faqs.a: Talk to the Assessor at (920) 832-5850, then give the City Clerk notice of intent at least 48 hours before the first Board of Review meeting and file Objection Form PA-115A in the first two hours of that meeting.

faqs.q: Who pays the Wisconsin transfer fee when an Appleton home sells?
faqs.a: The seller. The fee is 30 cents per $100 of value and the Register of Deeds collects it at recording. Transfers by inheritance, foreclosure deeds and some family conveyances are exempt.

faqs.q: Can I pay property tax under protest instead of appealing?
faqs.a: No. Paying under protest is not an objection unless you first filed an appeal with the Board of Review. The objection has to happen in spring, before the December bill arrives.
